```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = FALSE

```

Population simulation and estimation solve the same small ODE system for
many subjects.  The `gpu*` methods integrate every subject that is waiting
to be integrated at the same time: one OpenCL kernel launch with one
work-item per subject, after the per-trajectory design of Julia's DiffEqGPU
(Utkarsh et al. 2024).  Doses, steady state, lag times, covariates and
resets stay on the host and run rxode2's usual per-subject event code, so
any event table that works with a host method works here.

## Methods

| GPU method | Host counterpart | Integrator | Julia DiffEqGPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"gpuT54"` | `"t54"` | Tsitouras 5(4) | `GPUTsit5()` |
| `"gpuVern76"` | `"vern76"` | Verner 7(6) | `GPUVern7()` |
| `"gpuRos54p"` | `"ros54p"` | Rodas5P with the analytic Jacobian | `GPURodas5P()` |
| `"gpuT54+gpuRos54p"` | `"t54+ros54p"` | AutoSwitch on the device | -- |
| `"gpuVern76+gpuRos54p"` | `"vern76+ros54p"` | AutoSwitch on the device | -- |

The host counterpart solves any model with the same integrator, so a model
can move between the two without changing its numerical method.

## Requirements

- The suggested `OpenCL` package (with an OpenCL driver for your GPU, or
  pocl for CPUs) for `gpuBackend = "opencl"`.  rxode2 itself links no
  OpenCL; without the package the methods still run with the CPU build.
- A device with double precision (`cl_khr_fp64`), or
  `gpuPrecision = "float"`.
- A model whose `d/dt()` can be written as device code:
  `rxModelVars(model)$flags["gpuSafe"]` is 1.  Random numbers, `linCmt()`,
  `matExp()`, user R functions and similar keep a model on the host.

```{r}
library(rxode2)
rxGpuInfo()
#> $available
#> [1] TRUE
#>
#> $fp64
#> [1] TRUE
#>
#> $devices
#>   index                    platform                         device type  fp64
#> 1     1                     rusticl            AMD Radeon Graphics  gpu FALSE
#> 2     2 Portable Computing Language cpu-haswell-AMD Ryzen 7 PRO ...  cpu  TRUE
```

## Simulating

```{r}
mod <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- log(1.2)
    tcl <- log(3)
    tv <- log(30)
    eta.ka ~ 0.2
    eta.cl ~ 0.1
    eta.v ~ 0.1
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl) * (wt / 70)^0.75
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    d/dt(depot) <- -ka * depot
    d/dt(center) <- ka * depot - cl / v * center
    cp <- center / v
  })
}

ev <- et(amt = 300, ii = 12, addl = 6) |>
  et(seq(0, 96, by = 2)) |>
  et(id = 1:20000)
ev$wt <- 70

sim <- rxSolve(mod, ev, method = "gpuRos54p")
```

The options, all in `rxControl()`:

- `gpuBackend`: `"auto"` (default) uses OpenCL when a device with the
  requested precision exists and otherwise the CPU build, on `cores`
  threads; `"opencl"` and `"cpu"` choose explicitly.
  `options(rxode2.gpuBackend = "cpu")` sets what `"auto"` picks.
- `gpuDevice`: the device index from `rxGpuInfo()`.
- `gpuPrecision`: `"double"` (default) or `"float"`; with `"float"` loosen
  `atol` and `rtol` (for example to `1e-5` and `1e-4`).
- `gpuBatch`: the most subjects in flight at once (default 16384).

Each subject keeps its own tolerances, so a per-subject `tolFactor` (or
`atolRtolFactor_()` from `nlmixr2est`) loosens only that subject.

## When a model cannot run on the device

Under `gpuBackend = "auto"` these solve on the host with a message: a model
that is not GPU-safe uses the host counterpart; `delay()` read outside
`d/dt()`, steady state in a `delay()` model, resampled covariates, or a
registered `rxRegisterDydtForce()` hook use the model's default method.  An
explicit `gpuBackend = "opencl"` or `"cpu"` stops `rxSolve()` with an error
instead.  Inside an `nlmixr2` fit such a solve always uses the host
counterpart, whatever `gpuBackend` says.

## Estimation with nlmixr2

`nlmixr2` passes `rxControl()` to every solve, so a fit uses a GPU method
by naming it there.  This model (from `bench/gpu-nlmixr2.R`) has a
saturable term in its elimination:

```{r}
library(nlmixr2)
pk <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- log(1.2)
    tcl <- log(3)
    tv <- log(30)
    temax <- log(0.5)
    eta.ka ~ 0.2
    eta.cl ~ 0.1
    eta.v ~ 0.1
    prop.sd <- 0.1
    add.sd <- 0.05
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl)
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    emax <- exp(temax)
    d/dt(depot) <- -ka * depot
    d/dt(center) <- ka * depot - cl / v * (1 + emax * center / (center + 50)) * center
    cp <- center / v
    cp ~ add(add.sd) + prop(prop.sd)
  })
}

set.seed(42)
ev <- et(amt = 300, ii = 12, addl = 2, cmt = "depot") |>
  et(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 30, 36)) |>
  et(id = 1:500)
sim <- rxSolve(pk, ev, addDosing = TRUE, returnType = "data.frame")
dat <- sim[, c("id", "time", "evid", "amt", "cmt", "sim")]
names(dat)[names(dat) == "sim"] <- "dv"
dat$dv[dat$evid != 0] <- 0

fit <- nlmixr2(
  pk, dat, "saem",
  control = saemControl(rxControl = rxControl(method = "gpuRos54p"))
)
fitHost <- nlmixr2(
  pk, dat, "saem",
  control = saemControl(rxControl = rxControl(method = "ros54p"))
)
```

With 500 subjects (`bench/gpu-nlmixr2.R`, the node described under
Timings, 8 threads, seconds):

| method | backend | SAEM | FOCEi |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `liblsoda` | host | 183 | 10.8 |
| `t54` | host | 175 | 2.9 |
| `ros54p` | host | 276 | 9.6 |
| `"t54+ros54p"` | host | 185 | 2.9 |
| `gpuT54` | CPU build | 191 | 4.6 |
| `gpuRos54p` | CPU build | 201 | 4.5 |
| `"gpuT54+gpuRos54p"` | CPU build | 186 | 4.6 |
| `gpuT54` | OpenCL | 294 | 3.9 |
| `"gpuT54+gpuRos54p"` | OpenCL | 294 | 16.6 |

- SAEM solves every subject's three chains together, so the GPU methods
  integrate about 1500 subjects per round.  Their CPU build fits in about
  the time of the host methods; `gpuRos54p` takes 201 s against 276 s for
  `ros54p`.
- A round of 1500 subjects is too small to fill the L40 and takes longer
  there (1.7 ms) than on 8 CPU threads (0.9 ms), so OpenCL is slower than
  the CPU build for this fit.
- FOCEi solves one subject at a time while it optimizes the etas, so a GPU
  method runs its host counterpart there.

## Timings

All timings are from one node: an NVIDIA L40 (OpenCL, double precision)
and an Intel Xeon Gold 6526Y with 8 threads for the host methods, the CPU
build and Julia's `EnsembleThreads`.  Julia's GPU column is DiffEqGPU's
`EnsembleGPUKernel` on CUDA.  Ensembles: Lorenz on `t` in `[0, 1]` and
Robertson on `[0, 1000]`, one parameter set per subject,
`atol = rtol = 1e-8`.  Times in ms.

### Kernels

One round integrating every subject over one interval
(`bench/gpu-runtime-julia.R`, medians of 5):

| problem | rxode2 / Julia method | subjects | rxode2 OpenCL | Julia CUDA | rxode2 CPU build | Julia threads |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| lorenz | `gpuT54` / `GPUTsit5` | 1e3 | 3 | 1.2 | 2 | 3.6 |
| lorenz | `gpuRos54p` / `GPURodas5P` | 1e3 | 8 | 4.2 | 5 | 40 |
| lorenz | `gpuT54` / `GPUTsit5` | 1e5 | 18 | 46 | 207 | 393 |
| lorenz | `gpuVern76` / `GPUVern7` | 1e5 | 14 | 40 | 124 | 266 |
| lorenz | `gpuRos54p` / `GPURodas5P` | 1e5 | 30 | 69 | 527 | 3810 |
| robertson | `gpuRos54p` / `GPURodas5P` | 1e5 | 21 | 56 | 322 | 2424 |

- At 1e5 subjects the rxode2 kernels are 2.3 to 2.9 times faster than
  DiffEqGPU's CUDA kernels and 9 to 18 times faster than the CPU build.
- At 1e3 subjects a launch costs more than the integration, and the CPU
  build is as fast as the device.
- The end states agree with Julia's CUDA ones to 7e-10 and its threaded
  ones to 3e-9.

### Whole solves

Whole `rxSolve()` calls, with setup, event handling and the output data
frame included (`bench/gpu-solve-julia.R`, medians of 3):

| problem | GPU / host method | subjects | rxode2 OpenCL | Julia CUDA | rxode2 host | Julia threads |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| lorenz | `gpuT54` / `t54` | 1e4 | 38 | 5 | 145 | 29 |
| lorenz | `gpuRos54p` / `ros54p` | 1e4 | 47 | 7 | 645 | 341 |
| robertson | `gpuRos54p` / `ros54p` | 1e4 | 42 | 5 | 170 | 213 |
| lorenz | `gpuT54` / `t54` | 1e5 | 197 | 41 | 2736 | 405 |
| lorenz | `gpuRos54p` / `ros54p` | 1e5 | 235 | 73 | 5546 | 3799 |
| robertson | `gpuRos54p` / `ros54p` | 1e5 | 207 | 53 | 3336 | 2399 |

- The GPU methods are 14 to 24 times faster than their host counterparts
  at 1e5 subjects, and `gpuRos54p` is 12 to 16 times faster than Julia's
  threaded `Rodas5P()`.
- Julia's whole CUDA solve is 3 to 5 times faster: most of rxode2's time
  is `rxSolve()`'s own per-subject setup and output, which every method
  pays, not the kernel.

### Population PK with dosing

`bench/gpu-poppk.R` simulates 50000 subjects with doses, covariates and
dense sampling, so each subject needs one round per record (171 for `pk2`,
114 for `tmdd`):

- `pk2`: two-compartment PK, oral doses then IV infusions, weight and a
  time-varying creatinine clearance (non-stiff);
- `tmdd`: target-mediated drug disposition with fast binding (stiff).

`atol = 1e-8`, `rtol = 1e-6`, times in ms.  "CPU build" is
`gpuBackend = "cpu"`.

| method | `pk2` | `tmdd` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `liblsoda` | 11506 | 23910 |
| `ros54p` | 19738 | 39092 |
| `"t54+ros54p"` | 15418 | 53742 |
| `gpuT54`, CPU build | 12197 | -- |
| `gpuRos54p`, CPU build | 12843 | 15022 |
| `"gpuT54+gpuRos54p"`, CPU build | 12536 | 18006 |
| `gpuT54`, OpenCL | 11951 | -- |
| `gpuRos54p`, OpenCL | 12195 | 10249 |
| `"gpuT54+gpuRos54p"`, OpenCL | 11669 | 13931 |

- On the stiff `tmdd`, `gpuRos54p` on the L40 is 2.3 times faster than
  `liblsoda` and 3.8 times faster than the host `ros54p`.
- On the non-stiff `pk2` every method takes about the same time: with a
  round per record the host event handling, not the integration, sets the
  time.
- Explicit methods are not practical for `tmdd` (`t54` took 24 s and
  `gpuT54` on the L40 22 s at 1000 subjects); the AutoSwitch composites
  detect the stiffness and switch to `ros54p`, as `liblsoda` switches to
  BDF.

## How it works

1. Each subject runs rxode2's per-subject event loop as a resumable state
   machine that stops whenever it needs its states integrated from one
   time to the next.
2. A round collects every waiting subject and integrates all of them at
   once: one kernel launch, or the same code compiled for the CPU on
   `cores` threads.  No R code runs between rounds.
3. The subjects take their new states, handle their next events, and the
   loop repeats until all are done.

On OpenCL a launch costs more than on CPU threads, so when no subject's
events depend on its states (observations, boluses and infusions with a
fixed rate or duration) a solve takes one launch instead of a round per
event interval.  Each subject's events run first without integrating, which
records every interval it needs and what its doses add; one launch then
integrates each subject's whole timeline, and the subjects run their events
again with the results.  The results are the same as the rounds'.
`options(rxode2.gpuTimeline = FALSE)` turns this off.

The kernel is generated from the model: its `d/dt()` (and, for
`gpuRos54p`, the analytic Jacobian) as OpenCL C, the integrator, and the
special functions the model calls.  It is compiled once per model, method
and device and cached for the session.

  multiple GPU platforms. *Comput Methods Appl Mech Eng* 419:116591.
- Steinebach G (2023). Construction of Rosenbrock-Wanner method Rodas5P
  and numerical benchmarks within the Julia Differential Equations
  package. *BIT Numer Math* 63:27.
